content: Fetal hydantoin syndrome was first identified by Meadow et al. in 1968. Subsequent studies by Manson and Frederic in 1973 and Hanson and Smith in 1975 further elucidated the teratogenic effects of hydantoin. This syndrome is characterized by altered growth and development in fetuses of epileptic mothers who take phenytoin or other hydantoin anticonvulsants during pregnancy. It is understood to result from the exposure of the fetus to anticonvulsant medications used to treat maternal seizure disorders. A potential association with the EPHX1 gene has also been suggested. Although the exact mechanism of phenytoin embryotoxicity is not fully understood, several possible pathways have been proposed. Phenytoin inhibits sodium and calcium channels, which act as membrane stabilizers. This inhibition leads to the release of free radicals, causing endothelial damage, myocardial depression, bradycardia, and ultimately fetal hypoxia. Additionally, phenytoin induces cytochrome P450 activation, resulting in the production of teratogenic free radicals through the metabolism of epoxides, folate, and vitamin K in the liver. The severity of abnormalities associated with fetal hydantoin syndrome varies significantly among affected infants. The characteristic features of fetal hydantoin syndrome include growth abnormalities such as intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), postnatal growth deficiency, and microcephaly. Performance abnormalities range from developmental delays and dull mental capacity to severe intellectual disability. Dysmorphic craniofacial features are common and include a short nose with a broad, depressed nasal bridge, inner epicanthic folds, mild ocular hypertelorism, ptosis of the eyelids, strabismus, a wide mouth, sutural ridging, and a short neck with mild webbing. Less commonly, cleft lip and palate, as well as limb anomalies such as hypoplasia of the nails and distal phalanges, are observed. These limb anomalies may also include an increased frequency of low-arch digital dermal ridge patterns and triphalangeal thumbs. Some children with these craniofacial and limb features may also present with major anomalies in other systems, including cardiac defects. There is an increased incidence of genitourinary and central nervous system anomalies, more severe limb reduction defects, and diaphragmatic hernia. Fetal hydantoin syndrome is thought to result from a combination of genetic and environmental factors. A common cause is the use of the anticonvulsant drug phenytoin (Dilantin) during pregnancy. The risk of fetal hydantoin syndrome is estimated to be 2–3 times higher in children of epileptic women taking anticonvulsant drugs compared to the general population. The risk of neurological impairment is estimated to be 1–11%, which is also 2–3 times higher than in the general population. The risk of oral clefts and cardiac anomalies is approximately five times higher in infants exposed to hydantoin in utero. Less frequently observed abnormalities include microcephaly, ocular defects, hypospadias, and umbilical or inguinal hernias. Both males and females are equally affected by fetal hydantoin syndrome. Common risk factors include fetal exposure to antiepileptic drugs, particularly phenytoin. There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening for fetal hydantoin syndrome. However, in cases of in utero exposure to phenytoin, screening through cytogenetic analysis and detailed morphological ultrasound is recommended. Common complications of fetal hydantoin syndrome include microcephaly, growth deficiency, congenital heart defects, and systemic abnormalities involving the nervous, renal, and gastrointestinal systems. The diagnosis of fetal hydantoin syndrome is based on clinical features and a history of phenytoin exposure during pregnancy. Ultrasound may aid in diagnosis, with findings suggestive of the syndrome including gastroschisis, sacral meningomyelocele, absence of upper or lower limbs, clubfoot, pectus carinatum, and dilated right or left heart with pericardial effusion. Echocardiography may reveal pulmonary or aortic valvular stenosis, coarctation of the aorta, patent ductus arteriosus, or ventricular septal defects. X-rays may show absence or hypoplasia of carpal, metacarpal, and phalangeal bones, nail hypoplasia, hyperphalangism, pseudohyperphalangism, adactyly, or biphalangeal digits. Amniocentesis may demonstrate low epoxide hydrolase activity. Treatment of individuals with fetal hydantoin syndrome depends on the specific manifestations of the disease. Those with congenital heart defects may require major corrective surgery shortly after birth. Individuals with relatively minor health problems may not require therapy. Patients with the syndrome require close monitoring of growth, psychomotor development, craniofacial evaluation, and cardiac function. Orthopedic surgery may be necessary for bone defects, neurosurgery for nervous system abnormalities, and surgical correction for cleft lip or palate. Preventive measures include switching from polytherapy to monotherapy with antiepileptic drugs before pregnancy, reducing serum concentrations of antiepileptic drugs to the lowest effective levels, supplementing with folate before pregnancy, and regular monitoring of antiepileptic drug levels, folate, and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) values. Counseling parents about the risks of pregnancy and malformations, as well as regular fetal monitoring via ultrasonography, is also recommended. Periodic health checks of psychomotor and physical development are essential for secondary prevention.
